diveTitle: What actually happens when you compress
diveSubtitle: The details that matter once you go beyond the basics.
dive1Title: Why do PDFs get so large in the first place?
dive1Desc: Text and vector graphics take up almost no space — the size is almost always driven by embedded images. A PDF exported from a scanner or a phone photo can easily hit tens of megabytes because each page is a full-resolution image, not compressed text.
dive2Title: Lossy vs. lossless — what we actually do
dive2Desc: We use lossy compression on embedded images, re-encoding them at a lower quality and resolution, since that's where nearly all the size reduction comes from. Text and vector content are left untouched — they're already compact and compress losslessly by default.
dive3Title: Compressing scanned PDFs vs. text PDFs
dive3Desc: A scanned PDF, made entirely of images, compresses dramatically — often 70-90% smaller — because there's a lot of image data to optimize. A PDF that's mostly text with a couple of small images has little left to compress, so the reduction will be modest by comparison.
dive4Desc: If a PDF's images were already heavily compressed before being embedded, common with PDFs exported from other online tools, there's not much redundancy left to squeeze out. Re-compressing an already-compressed image mostly just adds generation loss without much size benefit.
dive5Desc: At our standard compression level, the quality loss is tuned to be invisible on screen and in most print output. For documents you plan to print at large sizes or professional quality, it's worth reviewing a page or two before distributing widely.
dive6Desc: You can upload and compress several PDFs in the same batch — each is compressed independently and returned as its own file. Compression ratio varies per file since it depends on each PDF's own image content, not a fixed percentage applied to everything.
faqSubtitle: Everything you need to know about compressing PDF files.
faq1Question: How much can I reduce my PDF file size?
faq1Answer: It depends on what's in the PDF. Files heavy with images can shrink by up to 90%. Text-only documents typically see 20–40% reduction. The Extreme mode gives the smallest file; Balanced keeps quality high.
faq2Question: Will the compressed PDF look different?
faq2Answer: In Balanced mode, the difference is barely noticeable — text stays crisp and images look clean. Extreme mode does reduce image quality slightly, but it's a big size win if that's what you need.
faq3Question: Can I compress more than one PDF at a time?
faq3Answer: Yes — the free plan lets you compress up to 2 PDFs at once. Upgrade to Starter for up to 10 files per batch, or Pro for unlimited batch processing. We process them all together and give you a zip file to download when there's more than one.
faq4Question: Is there a file size limit?
faq4Answer: On the free plan, each file can be up to 20MB (100MB on Starter). If yours is bigger, try splitting it first with our PDF splitter tool, then compress the parts.
faq5Question: What happens to my files after compression?
faq5Answer: Everything is deleted within one hour of processing. Your files are encrypted during the upload and transfer. We don't read them, keep them, or share them.
seoTitle: When You Need to Shrink a PDF
seoP1: Large PDFs are a pain to email, slow to upload, and eat up storage. Whether it's a scanned document, a presentation packed with images, or a form that's ballooned in size — our compressor handles it without you needing to install anything.
seoP2: You choose how aggressive the compression is. Maximum Quality mode (20–40% reduction) keeps everything looking sharp. Balanced (40–70%) is the go-to for most files. Extreme (70–90%) gives you the smallest possible file when size matters more than perfect image quality.
seoP3: Scanned documents, forms, presentations, ebooks, contracts — if it's a PDF, we can compress it. Our tool works across all devices: desktop, tablet, and phone. No app download required.
